title: YouCoded's look, round 2: four complete directions

steps.headline: Which directions are worth taking further? Pick any that excite you.
steps.notice: This is the shortlist. Everything after this compares the same piece across all four, so you can also mix: one direction's tray icon with another's website, for example.

variants.label: Built by you
variants.summary: Everything is made from one rounded block. Five blocks make the mascot, and each block stands for part of the product: head = the AI model, arms = skills, feet = where it runs, colour = your theme. The same blocks spell the name.
variants.risk: The block lettering is techy; a few letters (y, d) look unusual and some people will find it cold.

variants.label: Say it
variants.summary: You build YouCoded by talking to it, so its head is a speech bubble. Its face shows what it's doing: eyes when listening, dots when working, a tick when done. Warm serif headlines.
variants.risk: Speech bubbles are everywhere (Messenger, Discord), so at a glance it can read as a chat app.

variants.label: Stick it anywhere
variants.summary: Yours like the stickers on your laptop. The logo is a die-cut sticker of the waving mascot you picked in September; every theme is another sticker to collect.
variants.risk: Young and loud. Next to serious tools some people will read it as a kids' app.

variants.label: Choose your player
variants.summary: Your assistant is a character you pick, like a game's character select. Themes are skins. Drawn on a pixel grid, so it's sharp at every size.
variants.risk: Reads as gaming or retro, which works against 'for everyone'.

steps.headline: Which app icon and installer would you want on your taskbar?
steps.notice: The installer is the file people download first, so it's their first look at the brand.

variants.label: Built by you
variants.risk: At 16 and 24 pixels it's a separate simplified drawing, so the taskbar icon differs slightly from the Dock's.
variants.summary: Cream mascot with tangerine arms and feet on a purple tile. Installer: a flat-pack cardboard box.

variants.label: Say it
variants.risk: In a busy taskbar it may read as 'a messaging app' before 'an assistant'.
variants.summary: White speech-bubble face on a purple tile. Installer: the same icon with a small mint download bubble.

variants.label: Stick it anywhere
variants.risk: Yellow, not purple: your first-glance colour changes. The peeling corner may look odd among the Mac's flat icons.
variants.summary: Purple waving mascot stuck on a yellow sticker with a peeling corner. Installer: the sticker half-peeled off its sheet.

variants.label: Choose your player
variants.risk: The dark tile fades into a dark taskbar or Dock; only the purple mascot stands out.
variants.summary: Pixel-art mascot on a dark pixel tile. Installer: a game cartridge with the mascot on its label.

steps.headline: Which tray icon works best next to the clock?
steps.notice: The app has no tray icon today; your earlier screenshot was its taskbar button. Whichever wins gets built as a new feature.

variants.label: Built by you
variants.risk: The coloured 'needs you' dot can't be shown on a Mac, where tray icons must be one colour.
variants.summary: Just the head, white or black to match the bar. Eyes glance left and right while working.

variants.label: Say it
variants.risk: The 'done' tick face is rough at 16 pixels.
variants.summary: The bubble face, white or black. Eyes when idle, dots while working, a tick when done.

variants.label: Stick it anywhere
variants.risk: Boxy at this size: reads as 'little robot waving' more than 'sticker'.
variants.summary: The waving mascot as a one-colour silhouette. A coral dot means it needs you.

variants.label: Choose your player
variants.summary: The full mascot drawn pixel by pixel, white or black. It blinks and bobs while working.

steps.path: The first screen of the website
steps.headline: Which website first screen makes you want to download it?
steps.notice: Shown with today's headline and sub-line wherever the direction didn't write its own.

variants.label: Built by you
variants.risk: 'Parts' and 'assembly' talk can feel aimed at engineers or toy collectors.
variants.summary: 'Built by you.' beside a pulled-apart mascot diagram that labels each part as a feature.

variants.label: Say it
variants.summary: Soft serif headline beside a short chat: planning a week around exams.

variants.label: Stick it anywhere
variants.risk: The busiest of the four: lots competing for your eye.
variants.summary: 'yours.' as a coral sticker, beside a laptop lid covered in theme stickers.

variants.label: Choose your player
variants.risk: Dark and game-like: office users may not see a work tool.
variants.summary: A game's character-select screen: pick your mascot and skin.

steps.headline: Which help page feels most trustworthy while still being us?
steps.notice: These are the 'clinical' pages: privacy, setup and technical help. They must calm down without looking like a different company.

variants.label: Built by you
variants.summary: Plain page with a short at-a-glance table at the top.

variants.label: Say it
variants.summary: Serif headings, an 'In short' box and a two-step diagram of where messages go.

variants.label: Stick it anywhere
variants.risk: The calm page and the loud homepage can feel like two different companies.
variants.summary: Calm page with a 'short version' note and one small sticker in the margin.

variants.label: Choose your player
variants.risk: The pixel name in the header is harder to read than normal type.
variants.summary: Paper-white page; pixel touches only in the logo and small labels.

steps.path: How the logo changes with a theme
steps.headline: Which one keeps 'make it yours' while still being clearly YouCoded?
steps.notice: Every direction writes one rule for theme makers: what must stay, what's free to change.

variants.label: Built by you
variants.summary: Themes as toy packs. Always the same: five blocks, the gaps, the name. Free: colour, face, finish, one extra.

variants.label: Say it
variants.risk: Bubble shape is simple, so themes lean on colour and texture more than costume.
variants.summary: Six outfits. Always the same: the bubble, its tail-foot, a face up top. Free: everything else.

variants.label: Stick it anywhere
variants.summary: A sheet of theme stickers. Always the same: square head, two feet, the wave, the white edge.

variants.label: Choose your player
variants.risk: Every theme has to be drawn as pixel art, a skill fewer theme makers have.
variants.summary: A collection screen of skins. Always the same: the outline and where the eyes sit.

steps.headline: Which direction should round 3 develop into the finished brand?
steps.today: YouCoded uses three different mascot drawings, several ways of writing its name, and a blurry, low-contrast app icon.
steps.problem: Without one direction, every new page, icon and post invents its own look, and people can't recognise YouCoded from one place to the next.
steps.proposal: Round 3 takes one direction (or a mix you name) and finishes it: final logo files, icon sets for Windows, Mac, Linux and Android, website and help-page styles, and a one-page rulebook for theme makers.

options.label: Built by you
pros: The mascot's parts explain the product: you pick the model, skills, look
'Swap any part, still YouCoded' is exactly the rule themes need
Keeps the purple and the mascot you already have
cons: Block lettering can feel techy or cold
Needs gentler words than 'parts' and 'assembly' for everyday users

options.label: Say it
pros: Warmest and most grown-up; help pages feel trustworthy
Clearest tray icon, and its face shows what it's doing
cons: Can be mistaken for a chat app
Replaces the robot mascot people know

options.label: Stick it anywhere
pros: Builds on the waving, sticker-style mascot you chose in September
cons: Can read as a kids' product
Icon turns yellow instead of purple

options.label: Choose your player
pros: Strong 'pick and customise your character' story
cons: Themes have to be pixel art
